content:
## Analysis

### The problem

Every internal package is pinned to an exact version in `requirements.txt`. That means publishing a fix to an internal package has **zero effect** on production until a human manually edits `requirements.txt`, opens a PR, and gets it merged. The rollout notes confirm: *"None of the lag was build time; all of it was waiting for the edit."*

| Package | Fix published | Production still running | Lag |
|---|---|---|---|
| textutils | 2.3.7 (Jan 22) | 2.3.4 (reported Feb 12) | **21 days** |
| authkit | 1.9.2 (Jan 30) | 1.9.0 (reported Feb 14) | **15 days** |
| schemachk | 0.8.5 (Feb 2) | 0.8.1 (reported Feb 17) | **15 days** |
| metricsio | 3.1.4 (Jan 18) | 3.1.1 (reported Feb 9) | **22 days** |

### The fix

Stop pinning internal packages to exact versions. Use a **compatible-release** (`~=`) specifier so that a rebuild automatically pulls the latest patch release within a minor version series:

```
# Before (broken — blocks every fix):
textutils==2.3.4
authkit==1.9.0
schemachk==0.8.1
metricsio==3.1.1

# After (automatic patch uptake):
textutils~=2.3
authkit~=1.9
schemachk~=0.8
metricsio~=3.1
```

`~=2.3` means *any 2.3.x release ≥ the installed version*. A fix published as 2.3.7 is immediately available on the next `pip install -r requirements.txt` (i.e., the next CI build / deployment). No human needs to notice a release note.

If you prefer more explicit safety (e.g., not wanting `0.9` to cross into `0.10` automatically), use `>=` or `~=` with a lower bound that matches the fix version:

```
textutils>=2.3.7
```

### Why `==` was wrong for internal packages

`==` makes sense for third-party dependencies whose release cadence you don't control and whose changes might be breaking. Internal packages follow your own versioning convention and live in the same monorepo / registry — there is no reason to require a human middleman for every patch-level fix. Compatible-release specifiers (`~=`) are the standard PEP 440 mechanism for exactly this scenario.

Agreed, that is the lag. Decision: internal packages move to the compatible-release operator, so patch releases flow to a service on its next build without anyone editing a file or opening a pull request. Same minor series, patch level free. External dependencies keep their existing floor constraints; this changes only packages we publish ourselves.
